brief.head: Tyranny of the larks
brief.text: Amit Varma, a night owl, ac­cused Ajay Shah, a morn­ing lark, of com­plic­ity in “the tyranny of the larks”. About thirty per cent of peo­ple are night owls, he said. {100-R01}

brief.head: Read the party line
brief.text: A Federal Reserve of­fi­cial or some­one at a fi­nan­cial firm speaks within in­sti­tu­tional lim­its, Ajay Shah said. Behind con­strained writ­ing there is often “a full bub­bling mind”. {100-C05}

brief.head: Say it to the mirror
brief.text: Ajay Shah called pride a neg­a­tive emo­tion. Amit Varma said many women need more of it: “wake up every morn­ing and look in the mir­ror and say, I am awe­some.” {100-C06}

brief.text: A soft­ware en­gi­neer asked how to con­trib­ute to the world. Practise the craft, said Ajay Shah. If peo­ple pay you, Amit Varma added, you are adding value. {100-C24}

lead.kicker: Episode 100: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah take questions
lead.head: A century, and still not out

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 100

body: A hun­dred episodes ago, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah made what Shah called “a pact signed in blood”: they would find the bloody-mindedness to reach Episode 100, and then ask whether the show was worth doing. {#pact}

Shah’s ver­dict was yes, though a weekly show had been hard and he wor­ried about “creep­ing to the edges of ex­per­tise”. He apol­o­gised, gen­tle reader, if he had on oc­ca­sion mis­rep­re­sented his stan­dard er­rors.

Varma’s idea of the show had al­ways been looser: bring frames from one field to bear on an­other, and talk with­out pre­tend­ing to cer­tainty, as long as you are trans­par­ent that you are spec­u­lat­ing.
For the cen­tury they took readers’ ques­tions, tersely re­phrased by Shah, and an­swered them for an hour and a half, from bro­ken aca­demic in­cen­tives to sham­poo.
## Thoughtful peo­ple

The first ques­tion set the tone: what sep­a­rates thought­ful peo­ple from the rest? Self-reflection, Varma said. Once you in­ter­nalise it, it be­comes a vir­tu­ous cycle, and you seek out oth­ers who re­flect too.
Most peo­ple never do it, he said, es­pe­cially men. A friend of his, a CXO at a big com­pany, finds his fel­low ex­ec­u­tives have noth­ing to talk about but cricket, Bollywood and of­fice gos­sip.

Varma learnt his own eco­nom­ics and bi­ol­ogy with­out a de­gree in ei­ther. Find a field’s first prin­ci­ples, he said, such as scarcity, in­cen­tives or nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, and the rest of the field opens up.
“If it’s a rab­bit hole, just get into the rab­bit hole and the more you read and at some point the fog clears and you see the big­ger pic­ture,” he said. {100-C09}
Shah, who read bi­ol­ogy for plea­sure as a PhD stu­dent, finds that his work in­creas­ingly comes from other peo­ple: ar­gu­ing with them, and being cor­rected by them.
## Do the work
On cre­at­ing things, Varma was frank: 99 per cent of the things he had wanted to do, he had not done. {#undone} What he does have, he said, is a bias for ac­tion.
Asked how to build an au­di­ence on Substack, he called the ques­tion a trap. Beginners are bad, they get no au­di­ence, and if val­i­da­tion mat­ters they quit be­fore they get good. {100-C12}
Reading, he ar­gued, is how we col­lect the dots we join to pic­ture the world. “The more dots there are, the more high def­i­ni­tion our pic­ture will be.”
## India, and the end

On India, Shah was the op­ti­mist. For the first time in a cen­tury, he said, the coun­try is build­ing a crit­i­cal mass of in­tel­lec­tual ca­pac­ity, helped by the in­ter­net. “A coun­try can­not be bet­ter than its elite,” he said.
Varma had less faith in the elite. India’s de­fault re­li­gion, he said, is the re­li­gion of the state, and most young peo­ple still ex­pect it to solve every prob­lem.
Asked what part of Indian life is fa­tally mis­aligned with moder­nity, he named con­ven­tional mar­riage. For most of India, he said, “mar­riage is death for women”.
Asked how he keeps his hu­mour, Varma pointed to mor­tal­ity. Next to the cer­tainty of death, every other tragedy shrinks, and stress­ing over an ar­ti­cle be­comes laugh­able. {100-C22}
Shah’s ver­sion was to live fully and de­light in being alive. “Everything is ev­ery­thing,” he said, “and ev­ery­thing will die.”
And the show? It will go on, Varma said, “not be­cause we like the show”, but be­cause they like the com­pany.

second.label: Artificial intelligence
second.head: Mind the luggage rack
second.deck: Amit Varma toured Spain’s museums with ChatGPT, and found where to put his bag

pic.caption: The neoclassical Velázquez Door portico of the Museo del Prado, Madrid, in 2016
pic.credit: Emilio J. Rodríguez Posada, CC BY-SA 2.0

body: Travelling through Spain, Amit Varma had ChatGPT’s Deep Research write re­ports of some twenty thou­sand words be­fore each mu­seum: the Picasso Museum, the Prado, the Reina Sofia. Each set out the artists’ phases, the key works room by room, and the order to walk through them. {100-S08}
Before a train from Barcelona to Madrid, he asked where to put a huge bag. The AI asked which train, then named the coach and showed, with a pho­to­graph, the lug­gage racks at ei­ther end.
Judging AI by its cur­rent state, he said, is like judg­ing com­put­ing by a main­frame that filled a room in 1954. {100-C29} He still checks the sources. “A lot of it is how deeply you prompt.”

quote.text: So it’s a com­plete Google re­place­ment for me.

third.head: Late bloomers

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the widows who bloom

body: Amit Varma has re­cently seen sev­eral real cases of the same thing: an old woman whose hus­band has died sud­denly be­comes a new per­son. “It’s like she’s free, she’s bloom­ing, she’s learn­ing an in­stru­ment, or she’s trav­el­ling solo,” he said. {100-S09}
Such women may never have felt con­fined, he said: mar­riage was the struc­ture they flowed into, it was nor­malised, and no al­ter­na­tive ever seemed to exist.

Varma tied this to Chinmay Tumbe’s *India Moving*: the largest in­ter­nal mi­gra­tion in India hap­pens when women marry and move to the husband’s vil­lage. They lose their child­hood friends, and often even their names.

For most of India, Varma said, mar­riage de­stroys women’s agency and in­di­vid­u­al­ity. {100-C19} He granted that tra­di­tion has its re­as­sur­ances, and that find­ing love on dat­ing apps is deeply com­pli­cated too.

box.title: The century episode
box.text: The hosts held an ear­lier Ask Me Anything at Episode 50, the half­way mark. Readers sent ques­tions through a form, and Ajay Shah, who sorted them, re­phrased each one tersely. Amit Varma marked the mo­ment as one of “great cel­e­bra­tion, per­haps even great re­lief”. {100-R29}

sections.label: On learning
sections.head: Read a lot, forget a lot
sections.caption: reading, remembering and writing
body: What sep­a­rates thought­ful peo­ple from the rest? Amit Varma found it a lit­tle pompous to di­vide the world that way, but an­swered: self-reflection, which most peo­ple, es­pe­cially men, never do. {100-C02}
Six read­ers asked the same ques­tion: how do you re­mem­ber all this? Varma for­gets the de­tails within a week, keeps co­pi­ous notes in Roam Research, and lets vol­ume do the rest. {100-C10}
The risk is rep­e­ti­tion. He curses him­self for not read­ing enough, he said, each time he re­peats Bob Dylan’s “he not busy being born is busy dying”.
## Adjacencies

Ajay Shah added ad­ja­cen­cies. Topology be­wil­ders a new­comer but comes eas­ily after cal­cu­lus and real anal­y­sis, be­cause we re­mem­ber what con­nects richly to what we al­ready know. Each use of a mem­ory, he said, re­freshes it, like a static RAM cell.

On writ­ing, Varma uses the frame of stock and flow. Flow is blogs and col­umns, a writ­ing gym: he wrote some eight thou­sand blog posts from 2003 to 2008, none, he thinks, worth pre­serv­ing. {#posts} Stock is books, and he has not made enough.
Shah writes his col­umns and LEAP blog posts with a researcher’s push for nov­elty, so they be­come stock he can reuse. “So I feel books are the leap of in­te­gra­tion,” he said. {100-C14}

~ Shah drew a sober­ing les­son from academia, where pub­li­ca­tion bias re­wards sen­sa­tion and mil­lion-fold rises in re­search spend­ing have dis­ap­pointed: “When you put up re­ally high pow­ered in­cen­tives, the peo­ple will god­damn pur­sue them.”

quote.text: So if you just read a lot, the mem­o­rable stuff will stick with you, whether you take a note or not.

sections.label: On making
sections.head: Write first, audience later
sections.caption: doing the work
body: Amit Varma’s con­fes­sion was that he gets weekly shows done on dead­line and looks ef­fi­cient, while the books he deeply wants to write wait. The book he wrote in 2008 does not make him ter­ri­bly happy. {#book}
Asked how to build a Substack au­di­ence, he re­fused the premise. “A good prod­uct is the best mar­ket­ing,” he said. Write first; the au­di­ence comes later, or­gan­i­cally. {100-C12}

The hosts com­mit­ted to 104 episodes, two years, be­fore tak­ing a call on the show, know­ing they would be bad at first. {#pact104} Varma, who has “a face for audio”, keeps putting episodes out any­way.
## The thirty per cent

Nomsita, who sits be­hind the cam­era, asked how cre­ative peo­ple can nur­ture their souls and still earn a liv­ing. Varma, once a copy­writer, an MTV scriptwriter and a jour­nal­ist, said that if 70 per cent of your work is drudgery and 30 per cent sat­is­fies you, you are lucky. {100-C26}

Be bloody-minded about pro­tect­ing the thirty per cent, he said, and bring care to the drudgery, since that is where you learn the craft. As suc­cess comes, do not let the ratio drift to a hun­dred and noth­ing.
~ He has pushed friends the same way. Mohit Satyanand started a news­let­ter after one of Varma’s lec­tures on bias for ac­tion, and in about three years has not missed a Sunday. {100-S05}

quote.text: You’re very lucky to have that thirty per cent.

art.caption: Amit Varma on doing the work

sections.label: On India
sections.head: The state as a religion
sections.caption: India’s future
body: Ajay Shah is “very bullish” on politi­cians. Vijay Kelkar taught him that of­fi­cials are trained into con­ser­vatism while politi­cians are en­trepreneurs, walk­ing thou­sands of kilo­me­tres and know­ing far more about farm dis­tress and jobs than their slo­gans let on. {100-C03}
Amit Varma pushed back: if pol­i­tics is down­stream of cul­ture, pop­ulist de­mand will get pop­ulist sup­ply. Great lead­er­ship, Shah replied, is doing more than fol­low­ing the polls.
Shah is op­ti­mistic that the statism of the bad years from 1914 to 1945 is fad­ing as India glob­alises and grows com­fort­able with mar­kets. {#statism}

Varma, who meets more young peo­ple, dis­agreed. Most, he said, still look to the state as par­ent and provider and want it to fix every prob­lem. Because zero-sum, top-down think­ing is hard­wired, each gen­er­a­tion must fight the bat­tle anew. {100-C20}
## Maps keep chang­ing

Asked about na­tion-states, Varma noted that India has been one for only about 78 years. {#nation} Maps change all the time, he said, and the in­ter­net let both hosts swap com­mu­ni­ties of cir­cum­stance for com­mu­ni­ties of choice.
Shah named two high-probability trou­bles ahead: a dra­matic fall in fer­til­ity that will bring rapid age­ing, and global warm­ing that is al­ready baked in. {#fertility}
~ Varma would not call any­thing in­evitable. The world of 2040 can­not be pic­tured today, and that, for him, is a rea­son for hope.

quote.text: I find that the fact that it is un­known un­knowns is ac­tu­ally a cause of hope

sections.label: On living
sections.head: Play the hand you’re dealt
sections.caption: money, luck and mortality
body: Asked how to think about money, Ajay Shah of­fered one line: it is like blood. You need it to live, but it is not the way to keep score in the video game. {100-C15}
Amit Varma added that money feels like the bind­ing con­straint when you are young. Over a whole life, he said, the real scarcity is time: “That’s what you will def­i­nitely run out of.”

Five years of pro­fes­sional poker taught Varma to think in prob­a­bil­i­ties, which made him less cer­tain, less judge­men­tal and less proud of his suc­cesses. “I know that ninety nine per cent of ev­ery­thing is luck,” he said. {100-C07}
## No vic­tims

A reader asked what to do with­out the nur­tur­ing that shaped Shah. Everyone is dealt a ran­dom hand of cards, he replied, and the only in­ter­est­ing ques­tion is what you do next, not whin­ing about struc­tural in­jus­tice. {100-C23}
The worst thing a per­son can do, Varma said, is wrap them­selves in a nar­ra­tive of vic­tim­hood: your cir­cum­stances of birth do not de­fine you.
~ On hard times, Varma ad­vised cher­ish­ing small hap­pi­nesses and sol­dier­ing through. Nobody, he said, is a per­fectly ra­tio­nal man im­mune to the stormy forces of life.

quote.text: Money is like blood. You need money to live, but it’s not the point of liv­ing.

art.caption: Amit Varma on money, luck and mortality

quote.text: And the in­ter­net freed both of us, and cer­tainly for me it’s a very big deal that I could form com­mu­ni­ties of choice. And ge­og­ra­phy was no longer des­tiny

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: How the hosts learnt, quit, made pacts and lived through history

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on his education, formal and otherwise
stories.head: The six-lecture degree
body: Amit Varma’s de­gree is a BA in English lit­er­a­ture from Fergusson College in Pune. He at­tended, he reck­ons, about six classes in the three years com­bined. {100-S02}
Why lit­er­a­ture? “I only chose English lit­er­a­ture be­cause I knew I wouldn’t have to study,” he said. He coasted through those years, end­lessly cu­ri­ous and read­ing a lot.

His real ed­u­ca­tion came one first prin­ci­ple at a time. Steven Pinker’s *The Blank Slate* was his gate­way to nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, after which he read all of Richard Dawkins, *The Selfish Gene*, *The Blind Watchmaker*, “the whole she­bang”, and then Daniel Dennett and Robert Wright. {100-R03}
He quoted Douglas Adams, who said that once he un­der­stood nat­u­ral se­lec­tion there was no need to be­lieve in God, pre­fer­ring the awe of knowl­edge to the awe of ig­no­rance.

Economics went the same way: Henry Hazlitt’s *Economics in One Lesson*, Frédéric Bastiat, and pop­u­lar books such as Tim Harford’s *The Logic of Life*. You need not run re­gres­sions, he said; you need scarcity and in­cen­tives to be­come part of how you think. {100-R05}
He has used eco­nomic think­ing to break down cricket strat­egy. Then there were five years of pro­fes­sional poker, which taught him to think in a Bayesian way.
~ It was al­ways fun, he said, never work: find a new sub­ject, dive in, and do not ask what pro­duc­tive thing will come out of it. That, he thinks, is how most peo­ple are.
stories.why: Credentials are not the gate. Once a field’s first prin­ci­ples click, whether scarcity and in­cen­tives or nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, the rest of the field opens up, and its tools can be car­ried else­where, as Varma car­ried eco­nom­ics into cricket. {100-C09}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on his six classes

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a writers’ pact made in Kochi
stories.head: The boat stayed, one book sailed
body: Two years ago, at a con­fer­ence in Kochi, Amit Varma, Lancelot Pinto and Vasant Dhar were taken to a boat for a ride. A storm started, and the boat never went any­where. {100-S06}
So they stood on the boat, look­ing out at the water, talk­ing about the books each of them wanted to write. They made a pact: by the next year’s con­fer­ence, all three would have writ­ten one.

Varma had ear­lier pushed Dhar to start a news­let­ter in a per­sonal tone, then to write a book in that voice. Two years on, Dhar has just sent his final man­u­script to his pub­lisher. {#manuscript}
~ Varma and Pinto have not. Whenever they meet, they mar­vel at Vasant, and hope to be in­spired by him.

quote.text: by the time this con­fer­ence comes about next year, all three of us would have writ­ten a book

stories.postscript: Ajay Shah and Akshay Jaitly, both sur­rounded by friends who write books, each plan a shelf of signed copies only. {100-S07}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on a pact made on a boat in Kochi

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on living through history as it happened
stories.head: Front-row seat to every crisis
body: Ajay Shah never ac­cepted the nar­row track where you spe­cialise and ori­ent your­self to pub­li­ca­tion. As a PhD stu­dent, he was end­lessly read­ing bi­ol­ogy on the side.

Looking back, he sees one deep dive into a global drama after an­other: the Asian cri­sis, 9/11 and Islamic ex­trem­ism, the Afghanistan wars, the 2008 fi­nan­cial cri­sis, the pan­demic and mod­ern pop­ulism. “So I’m the child of all these big global dra­matic events that hap­pened,” he said. {100-S04}
Amit Varma re­called the old Chinese curse, may you live in in­ter­est­ing times. For Shah it seemed a bless­ing, Varma said, “which can only mean you’re a so­ciopath”. {100-J05}

~ Shah said he was thrilled to have lived through it. Reading about the Great Depression is dif­fer­ent, he said, from being there: watch­ing the data, know­ing who said what on which date, being sur­prised when the VIX crossed 68. {#vix}
stories.why: A broad base in sci­ence, sta­tis­tics, eco­nom­ics and his­tory gives you entry gates into each new cri­sis, Shah said. With them, every un­fold­ing event be­comes a live sem­i­nar rather than a head­line.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on a life of global dramas

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the job he decided never to have
stories.head: Notice served, for good
body: Around 2006 or 2007, Amit Varma was man­ag­ing ed­i­tor of Cricinfo. Some sev­en­teen years ago, he said, he de­cided he would never do a job again. {100-S03}

He moved to a con­sult­ing role as con­tribut­ing ed­i­tor for a cou­ple of years, then left en­tirely. He wrote a book, played pro­fes­sional poker for five years and edited *Pragati*, a pol­icy mag­a­zine, for the Takshashila Institution, re­motely and part-time.
The choice, he said, did not al­ways seem like good for­tune. But it gave him time to read what he wants, when he wants, with­out being pushed down par­tic­u­lar tracks.

~ He has not been as in­ten­tional about the knowl­edge life as he would like, he ad­mit­ted, and Ajay Shah has done bet­ter. When a guest has writ­ten eight books, Varma reads all eight. {#eightbooks}

quote.text: I was never a com­pany man, and that gives me the time to read when I want, read what I want.

quiz.q: In a single line on money, what did Ajay Shah compare it to?

quiz.q: Which book did Varma cite for the claim that roughly thirty per cent of people are night owls?
quiz.a: *Why We Sleep* by Matthew Walker, which Varma called an ex­cel­lent book.

quiz.q: According to Chinmay Tumbe’s book, as cited by Amit Varma, what causes India’s largest internal migration?
quiz.a: Marriage: women move from their own vil­lage to their husband’s vil­lage.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 100. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Bob Dylan (Raph_PH, CC BY 2.0); Museo del Prado (Emilio J. Rodríguez Posada, CC BY-SA 2.0); Steven Pinker (Christopher Michel, CC BY-SA 4.0); Richard Dawkins (David Shankbone, CC BY 3.0); Charlie Munger (Nick, CC BY 2.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Apple and Open Library.

shelf.title: Why We Sleep
shelf.creator: Matthew Walker
shelf.why: The book that taught Amit how un­der­rated sleep is: with­out it you can’t be your best self, sleep-deprived driv­ers are more dan­ger­ous than drunk ones, and night owls, roughly 30% of peo­ple, sim­ply run on a dif­fer­ent rhythm.

shelf.title: Superforecasting
shelf.creator: Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner
shelf.why: A mas­ter­ful primer on prob­a­bilis­tic think­ing: TV ex­perts, re­warded for ex­ud­ing cer­tainty, are often wrong, while good fore­cast­ers keep up­dat­ing their pri­ors.

shelf.title: The Blank Slate
shelf.creator: Steven Pinker
shelf.why: Amit’s gate­way into nat­u­ral se­lec­tion and evo­lu­tion­ary psy­chol­ogy: Pinker ex­am­ines human na­ture and so­ci­ety through our evo­lu­tion­ary hard­wiring.

shelf.title: Richard Dawkins’s books, including The Selfish Gene and The Blind Watchmaker
shelf.creator: Richard Dawkins
shelf.why: He read ‘the whole she­bang.’ Understanding nat­u­ral se­lec­tion deeply changed how he sees human na­ture.

shelf.title: Economics in One Lesson
shelf.creator: Henry Hazlitt
shelf.why: Hazlitt’s 1946 ‘col­lec­tion of light bulbs’ that uses the ba­sics of scarcity and in­cen­tives to clear up fal­la­cies about price con­trols, tar­iffs, in­fla­tion and gov­ern­ment spend­ing, teach­ing you to ask what the money would have done if left with con­sumers.

shelf.title: The writings of Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: The writ­ings of ‘the man who re­ally turned me on to freedom’, as Amit puts it: Bastiat put com­plex eco­nomic ideas into sim­ple lan­guage with­out dumb­ing them down, and gives you a frame­work for see­ing the world.

shelf.title: The Logic of Life
shelf.creator: Tim Harford
shelf.why: Popular eco­nom­ics that shows how eco­nomic rea­son­ing ex­plains ev­ery­day life.

shelf.title: The Language Instinct
shelf.creator: Steven Pinker
shelf.why: He calls it a great book on how the struc­tures of lan­guage are built into the brain.

shelf.title: India Moving
shelf.creator: Chinmay Tumbe
shelf.why: Amit calls it one of the great books of the last ten years.

shelf.title: Aella’s Substack
shelf.creator: Aella
shelf.why: Aella’s Substack, one of the few news­let­ters Amit pays for: strong data work on young people’s sex­ual lives from a for­mer sex worker who is also a very good data sci­en­tist, ‘so packed with insight’ about gen­der re­la­tions.

shelf.title: Signull’s newsletter
shelf.creator: Signull
shelf.why: The qual­ity of the con­tent, which he finds gen­uinely thought-provoking.

shelf.title: Mohit Satyanand’s newsletter
shelf.creator: Mohit Satyanand
shelf.why: About three years with­out miss­ing a Sunday.

shelf.title: Vasant Dhar’s newsletter
shelf.creator: Vasant Dhar
shelf.why: Amit be­lieved the per­sonal tone would re­ally work.

shelf.title: Brave New World
shelf.creator: Vasant Dhar
shelf.why: Vasant Dhar’s pod­cast, which Amit calls great and backs as the show of a very dear friend.

shelf.title: Shane Parrish’s books
shelf.creator: Shane Parrish
shelf.why: ‘Shane Parrish’s books are great.’ A good source for build­ing a tool­kit of men­tal mod­els.

shelf.title: Charlie Munger’s wisdom
shelf.creator: Charlie Munger
shelf.why: Munger has al­ways been a source of great wis­dom on how to think.

shelf.title: Just (song and music video)
shelf.creator: Radiohead
shelf.why: There’s so much more to Radiohead than Creep.

shelf.title: Amit’s column on the benefits of reading books
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Sets out his ar­gu­ment that books mul­ti­ply the dots we join to pic­ture the world, let­ting us live many lives.

shelf.title: ChatGPT Deep Research
shelf.creator: OpenAI
shelf.why: Amit calls it ‘off the charts good’: it asks clar­i­fy­ing ques­tions, cites sources and writes deep cus­tom re­ports, and has re­placed Google for him, down to build­ing an art-history guide to each mu­seum he vis­ited.

shelf.title: Roam Research
shelf.why: Amit’s note-taking tool, which he calls a game changer: nested en­tries and two-way links turn any term into a hub of re­lated notes, re­plac­ing his scroll-and-search Word files and mak­ing up for a mem­ory he says isn’t great.

shelf.title: Professional cycling as a sport to follow
shelf.why: It gives all the drama and sto­ries of sport for far less time than cricket.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode: Fixing the Knowledge Society
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why academia has drifted away from real-world prob­lems: jour­nal-based pro­mo­tion and de­part­men­tal in­cen­tives nar­row every dis­ci­pline, fil­ter out cre­ative mav­er­icks and leave aca­demics writ­ing for each other.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on economic fallacies
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How in­stincts evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes mis­lead us in large, com­plex so­ci­eties: zero-sum think­ing, top-down think­ing, blind­ness to spon­ta­neous order and the pull of strong lead­ers.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on atheism
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: ‘Awesome episode, I’m very proud of it.’

shelf.title: Everything is Everything Episode 49 (on podcasting) and the productivity episode
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s fullest think­ing on the craft of pod­cast­ing, which Ajay says also ex­plains how the mod­ern media and cre­ative economies work.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on whether character is contingent
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: On whether char­ac­ter is con­tin­gent and whether we can ever know our­selves: a small change in brain chem­istry, as with Phineas Gage, can make you a dif­fer­ent per­son.

shelf.title: Episode 50: Ask Me ANYTHING!
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The com­pan­ion to this episode, recorded at the half­way mark.

laughs.text: After Ajay calls him­self a child of the Asian cri­sis, 9/11, 2008 and the pan­demic, Amit says: ‘There’s an old Chinese curse, may you live in in­ter­est­ing times. For you it seems a bless­ing which can only mean you’re a so­ciopath.’

Ajay gushes about grow­ing mush­rooms (‘my stom­ach is burst­ing with anticipation’), then ad­mits, ‘This is all the­o­ret­i­cal. I haven’t done it yet.’ Amit: ‘You must be a fungi.’ Later Ajay says Arvind Modi’s ex­cite­ment about tax pol­icy after forty years matches his own about mush­rooms, ‘and I haven’t even grown any mush­rooms.’ Amit: ‘Which is why you’re ex­cited.’

Asked whether he’d keep a seag­ull as a pet after once declar­ing ‘seag­ulls are bastards’, Amit replies: ‘If a seag­ull is a bas­tard, why would I keep a seag­ull as a pet?’ He’d keep Steven Seagal as a pet in­stead.
Bob Dylan, Amit’s favourite line about thought­less lives: ‘if you’re not busy being born, you’re busy dying.’
Thomas Watson, pres­i­dent of IBM, who fa­mously said ‘I think there’s a world mar­ket for three com­put­ers.’ Amit cites it as a warn­ing against judg­ing AI by its cur­rent state.
